screens.title: Animation Principles in Practice
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn three core animation tools that turn motion into meaning. Squash & Stretch gives objects a sense of volume and elasticity. Anticipation prepares the audience for a big action so it reads as believable. Follow Through and Overlapping Action add secondary motion and realistic settling after the main movement. Together, these principles let you express weight, timing, and personality for characters and props in games and cinematic animation. We'll focus on practical Maya workflows — keyframing Scale and Translate attributes, using the Graph Editor to offset curves, and assessing timing through playblasts. You'll work with a simple bouncing ball and short examples like a jump or a punch so you can see cause and effect. A common mistake is changing scale on only one axis and breaking volume; you'll learn how to compensate other axes to preserve perceived volume. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to plan a short loopable animation that communicates an object's material and impact. Think about what emotion or weight you want a movement to convey before you keyframe; that intent guides every squash, wind-up, and follow-through.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Animation Principles
Animation Principles in Practice
Squash & Stretch • Anticipation • Follow Through

These three principles let you shape how an audience reads motion. You will see practical Maya techniques for scale keyframes, timing, and offsetting curves so motion reads with weight and personality. Examples include a deformable bouncing ball, a crouch-to-jump, and a ponytail settling after a run.

In this lesson
Understand and apply three principles to create expressive, loopable animations.
Why it matters
Clear animation improves readability and player feedback in games.
What you'll practice
Keyframing Scale and Translate, timing anticipation, offsetting secondary motion.
Outcome
A short bouncing-ball animation demonstrating all three principles.
Concept Map
Squash & Stretch, Anticipation, Follow Through — small linked cards showing how each affects timing and emotion.
Squash & Stretch
Anticipation
Follow Through
Explore Key Topics
Squash & Stretch: use scale keyframes to show material and impact, preserving apparent volume.
Anticipation: a small opposing movement before a main action to cue the viewer.
Follow Through: stagger secondary motion so parts continue after the main movement ends.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to name, implement, and combine Squash & Stretch, Anticipation, and Follow Through to make motion readable and expressive. The first objective is to understand these principles conceptually: know what each principle claims about motion and why it matters for weight and personality. Second, you will apply Squash & Stretch by keyframing Scale attributes in Maya while preserving perceived volume. Third, you will implement Anticipation to cue an audience with a small opposing motion that makes primary actions feel powerful. Fourth, you will use Follow Through and Overlapping Action to offset secondary elements using the Graph Editor so motion settles naturally. Each objective includes a short why-it-matters note and a verification milestone, for example a playblast of a bouncing ball that exhibits squash, a crouch-to-jump with anticipation, and a ponytail or flag demonstrating overlapping action. These skills are practical for game-ready loops and quick feedback animations, and they help you communicate intent clearly in short animation cycles.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practice
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen ties each skill to a short Maya exercise you can complete to verify understanding. For Squash & Stretch, the milestone is a bouncing ball with scale keys at impact and peak that preserve volume. For Anticipation, the milestone is a short crouch or wind-up preceding a jump or punch by a few frames, timed so the main action reads clearly. For Follow Through and Overlapping Action, the milestone is a secondary element like a ponytail, flag, or pendulum that is offset in time and settles after the primary motion. Use the Graph Editor to refine tangency and curve shapes. These exercises are practical checks: if your motion reads on a quick playblast and communicates weight and intent without explanation, you have achieved the learning goals.

screens.title: What these principles accomplish
screens.narratorSegment: Animation principles are not decorative rules; they are tools for communicating physical and emotional information. When you apply Squash & Stretch, you answer questions about material and impact — is an object soft and bouncy or hard and heavy? Anticipation sets audience expectations so a major action is readable rather than jarring. Follow Through and Overlapping Action supply believable secondary motion so limbs, hair, or fabric behave with inertia and delay. Together these principles form a language: timing determines how quickly intent is communicated, deformation shows elasticity, and offset motion signals continuity. For example, a heavy object will have minimal stretch and a short, shallow anticipation, whereas a light object can stretch more and use a longer, more exaggerated anticipation. A common misconception is that more deformation always equals better animation — in truth, the amount of squash or stretch must match the perceived material and the scene's intent. As you plan an animation, state the intended weight and emotion first, then choose how much deformation, how long the anticipation lasts, and how much lag to apply in overlapping components. That planning keeps each keyframe purposeful and the performance readable.

keyIdea.title: Principle summary
keyIdea.text: These rules are communicative choices: match deformation, timing, and lag to the object’s weight and the action’s intent.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What these principles accomplish
Definition
These principles make motion readable: deformation, preparation, and secondary motion communicate weight and intention.
• Squash & Stretch shows elasticity and impact by deforming an object's silhouette while preserving apparent volume.
• Anticipation cues the audience with a small opposing action so the main motion feels deliberate.
• Follow Through and Overlapping Action stagger motion so parts continue and settle after the main action.
Key Takeaway

Treat these rules as intentional choices: pick amounts and timing that match material and emotion.

Concrete example — compare a heavy vs light ball
Heavy ball
Minimal squash on impact, short anticipation, subtle follow through—feels dense and sluggish.
Light rubber ball
Pronounced stretch on launch, bigger squash at impact, longer rebound and wobble during follow-through.
Common misconception: bigger deformation always improves animation. Instead, deformation must match intent—exaggeration supports communication, not arbitrary distortion.

screens.title: Squash & Stretch
screens.narratorSegment: Squash & Stretch is the most visual of these principles. It modifies an object's scale to show compression on impact or extension during fast motion. The essential constraint is volume preservation: if the object squashes vertically, the horizontal axes must expand proportionally so the silhouette's perceived volume stays consistent. In Maya, you animate Scale Y for vertical compression and Scale X/Z to compensate horizontally. For instance, when a rubber ball hits the ground, you would key a decreased Scale Y at the impact frame and increased Scale X and Scale Z at that same frame, then return to neutral scale at frames just before and after. When the ball leaves the ground, the reverse occurs: Scale Y increases for stretch, and Scale X/Z decrease. A common error is scaling just one axis, which makes the object appear to gain or lose volume and undermines the illusion of a cohesive material. A practical rule is to plan the maximum deformation, then distribute compensation across the other axes so perceived volume holds. This produces convincing impacts and elastic motion without breaking believability.

keyIdea.title: Squash & Stretch core
keyIdea.text: Deform while preserving apparent volume; scale opposite axes to maintain believable mass and material.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Squash & Stretch
Principle
Deforming an object to show compression and extension while preserving perceived volume.
• Preserve apparent volume: compensate other axes when one axis scales.
• Use squash at impact, stretch during quick motion or launch, neutral at rest.
• Amount of deformation depends on material: soft objects squash more than hard ones.
Key Takeaway

Always compensate axes to keep the object's perceived volume consistent during deformation.

Maya implementation — practical steps
Impact frame
Keyframe Scale Y to a smaller value and key Scale X/Z to larger values at impact; return to 1.0 before and after.
Launch frame
Keyframe Scale Y larger for stretch and scale X/Z smaller as the object accelerates upward.
Example values
Impact: Scale Y = 0.7, Scale X/Z = 1.2. Stretch: Scale Y = 1.2, Scale X/Z = 0.9. Neutral: all = 1.0.
Common mistake: only changing Scale Y. That breaks volume and makes the object appear to grow or shrink instead of deforming.

screens.title: Keyframing Squash & Stretch in Maya
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk a simple step-by-step process to add squash and stretch to a bouncing ball in Maya. Start with a Polygon Sphere and animate Translate Y to create a basic 48-frame bounce that impacts the ground and rebounds 2–3 times. Identify the impact frames where the sphere contacts the ground and the peak frames at the top of each bounce. At each impact frame, key Scale Y to a smaller value such as 0.7 and key Scale X and Scale Z to larger values such as 1.2. Immediately before and after the impact frame, key all scales back to 1.0 so the deformation reads as a quick compression. At the frames where the ball leaves the ground, do the reverse: increase Scale Y to 1.2 and reduce Scale X/Z to 0.9 for stretch. Use the Graph Editor to smooth tangents and give a crisp snap on impact with slightly steeper curves there. Playblast frequently to judge timing. If the ball feels like it changes mass, adjust compensation values across X and Z until volume reads stable. This practical loop will make the ball feel alive and responsive.

keyIdea.text: Key impact and peak scales, return to neutral around those frames, and refine with the Graph Editor and playblasts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Keyframing Squash & Stretch
Process
A repeatable sequence for the bouncing ball exercise.
  1. Create a Polygon Sphere and animate Translate Y for 48 frames with 2–3 bounces.
  2. Identify impact and peak frames for each bounce.
  3. At impact: key Scale Y smaller (e.g., 0.7) and Scale X/Z larger (e.g., 1.2).
  4. Before/after impact: key all scales to 1.0 to neutralize the shape.
  5. At launch: key Scale Y larger and Scale X/Z smaller to show stretch.
  6. Refine tangents in the Graph Editor and playblast to check timing.
Concrete example values
Frame 12: Impact
  ScaleY = 0.7
  ScaleX = 1.2
  ScaleZ = 1.2
Frame 14: Post-impact
  ScaleX = 1.0
  ScaleY = 1.0
  ScaleZ = 1.0
Frame 16: Launch
  ScaleY = 1.2
  ScaleX = 0.9
  ScaleZ = 0.9
Frame 20: Peak
  ScaleX = 1.0
  ScaleY = 1.0
  ScaleZ = 1.0
Use the Graph Editor to sharpen the impact tangent so the squash hits quickly, and use smooth tangents on stretches for airy motion.
Pro tip

Playblast short loops often; small timing tweaks produce large differences in perceived weight.

screens.title: Common mistakes and fixes for Squash & Stretch
screens.narratorSegment: Animators often make a small set of repeatable mistakes when applying Squash & Stretch. The most damaging is scaling only one axis. That makes the object appear to gain or lose mass, breaking the viewer's suspension of disbelief. Another common error is an overly long squash or stretch — if the deformation lingers, the motion reads slow and gummy. Conversely, too brief an adjustment can be invisible. Fixes are straightforward: always compensate the other axes so perceived volume stays stable, and place neutral keys immediately before and after the extreme frame so deformation is a quick, readable impulse. Timing matters: use a sharper curve at impact to sell a snap, and longer, smoother tangents for stretches that imply speed and flexibility. For iterative testing, duplicate your layer or copy keys to compare 'without principles' and 'with principles' versions. This A/B comparison is powerful for seeing how much these small adjustments improve believability. Common mistakes and fixes for Squash & Stretch means compensate axes, use neutral keys around extremes, and adjust tangents to control snap versus stretch.. In practical terms, why volume preservation and timing matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Common mistakes & fixes
Mistakes
• Scaling a single axis only — breaks volume.
• Deformation that lingers — makes motion feel slow or rubbery.
• No neutral keys around extremes — deformation reads as an abrupt jump.
Warning

If volume feels inconsistent, the audience will perceive a change in object mass—this undermines believability.

Fixes
• Compensate other axes when scaling an axis to preserve volume.
• Insert neutral keys before and after extremes to make deformation a quick impulse.
• Use the Graph Editor: steep tangents for snap, soft tangents for smooth stretch.
Comparison exercise: duplicate your animation layer and toggle between versions with and without squash to see the difference in perceived weight.

screens.title: Anticipation
screens.narratorSegment: Anticipation is a preparatory movement that signals a forthcoming primary action. Think of a pitcher winding up, or a character crouching before leaping. Anticipation gives the viewer a moment to prepare and makes the subsequent movement read as purposeful and powerful. In practice, anticipation is a small, often opposite-direction movement placed a few frames before the main key action. Timing is the crucial variable—too long, and the action feels delayed; too short, and it doesn't register as a cue. For a jump, you might animate a brief downward translation combined with a slight compression of the body for two to four frames, then launch upward with a stronger key. For a punch, a subtle pull-back of the arm across one to three frames makes the thrust read with mass. A frequent misconception is that anticipation must be large to be effective. In reality, subtle opposition timed well is often more convincing than a long, exaggerated wind-up. Anticipation also helps combine with squash and stretch: a pre-launch compression can both cue the jump and set up a more pronounced stretch on takeoff.

keyIdea.title: Anticipation central idea
keyIdea.text: A brief opposing motion before the main action makes that action read as intentional and powerful.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Anticipation
Definition & timing
A preparatory motion that readies the audience and adds weight to the main action.
• Anticipation is usually short: 1–4 frames for snappy moves, longer for dramatic build-ups.
• It often moves opposite the main action: a small recoil before a forward thrust or a crouch before a jump.
• It can include deformation (slight squash) to suggest stored energy.
Why it matters

Anticipation prevents actions from feeling sudden and gives the viewer time to process intent.

Examples
Jump
Downward translation plus slight compression 2–4 frames before upward launch.
Punch
Arm pulls slightly back across 1–3 frames before a fast forward thrust.
Misconception: anticipation must be large. Subtle, well-timed cues are often more convincing than long wind-ups.

screens.title: Implementing Anticipation in Maya
screens.narratorSegment: To implement anticipation in Maya, start by identifying the main action and the frame where it begins. Insert a short opposing motion a few frames earlier. For example, if a jump's launch begins at frame 20, add a crouch that reaches its low point at frames 17–18, with slight scale compression and a downward Translate Y. Key all body or object attributes for that brief opposing pose. When the main action arrives, animate the strong forward motion and return scales to neutral at the peak. The key is timing: test 1–4 frames for small, snappy actions; extend to 6–10 frames for slower, dramatic setups. Use the Graph Editor to keep anticipation as a readable prep by shortening tangents on the prep pose so it snaps into the main motion. A practical workflow is to block the main poses first, add the anticipation, then refine interpolation. Remember that anticipation also interacts with Squash & Stretch: a pre-launch compression will make your stretch on takeoff more convincing. Misapplied anticipation that is too long or too large can distract from the action; always iterate with playblasts to read how the timing reads to a fresh eye.

keyIdea.text: Block main poses, insert a short opposing prep a few frames before action, then refine timing in the Graph Editor.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Implementing Anticipation
Workflow
Block, insert prep, refine with Graph Editor and playblasts.
• Find the main action start frame.
• Add a short opposing key 1–4 frames earlier for snappy moves, or longer for dramatic timing.
• Combine slight scale compression with Translate changes to suggest stored energy.
Check

If viewers miss the cue, shorten or increase the contrast of the prep until intent is clear.

Concrete example — jump
Frame 17: Crouch low (anticipation)
  TranslateY = -0.2
  ScaleY = 0.95
  ScaleX = 1.05
Frame 20: Launch (main action)
  TranslateY = +1.5
  ScaleY = 1.1
  ScaleX = 0.95
Frame 22: Peak
  TranslateY = +2.0
  Scale = 1.0
Tweak how many frames the crouch occupies and refine tangents so the prep snaps into the launch without feeling delayed.

screens.title: Follow Through & Overlapping Action
screens.narratorSegment: Follow Through and Overlapping Action give animated motion natural continuity. Follow Through is the continuation of motion after the main action stops—hair, clothing, or loose parts keep moving and then settle. Overlapping Action is the principle that different parts start and stop at slightly different times; the tip of a ponytail will lag the root, a hand will follow the arm, and cloth panels will react with a delay. To animate these, you offset keyframes for secondary elements so motion propagates rather than occurring simultaneously. This creates the illusion of inertia and prevents staccato, robotic movement. For instance, when a character stops running, the torso stops before the hair and jacket do; the secondary elements drag and then settle. A common pitfall is keyframing everything identically so all joints move in sync—this flattens the performance. Use small timing offsets and softening tangents so follow-through reads as a natural cascade rather than a separate animation layer. Follow Through & Overlapping Action means offset secondary motion in time and shape tangents so parts continue and settle after the main action.. In practical terms, adding realistic secondary motion and staggered timing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Follow Through & Overlapping Action
Definition
Secondary motion that continues after the primary action and moves with timing offsets.
• Follow Through: continuation and settling after the main movement ends.
• Overlapping Action: parts move at different times; some lead, others lag.
• Use offsets and softened tangents for natural cascades.
Key Takeaway

Stagger timing for secondary parts so motion reads as continuous and physically plausible.

Concrete example — ponytail or flag
Ponytail
Animate root movement, offset keyframes for each segment down the chain so the tip lags and then settles with damping.
Flag
Different parts of the fabric move with varying delay and amplitude to mimic wind and inertia.
Misconception: staggering keys equals sloppy animation. In fact, staggered timing makes motion appear deliberate and physically grounded.

screens.title: Animating Follow Through in Maya
screens.narratorSegment: Animating Follow Through and Overlapping Action in Maya is an exercise in timing offsets and curve shaping. Begin by animating the main body or root motion and set those key poses first. Then, select secondary controllers or joints and shift their keyframes later in time, increasing the offset progressively down a chain. For a ponytail, the root matches the torso, the mid segment is offset by a few frames, and the tip lags the most. Use the Graph Editor to soften tangents on secondary curves so motion eases rather than abruptly stopping. Add small oscillations with decreasing amplitude to simulate settling—this decay is what makes follow-through feel natural. If you animate everything simultaneously, the result will look stiff. Test by scrubbing and playing a short loop: the secondary parts should appear to drag and then damp out. keyIdea.title: Follow-through workflow
keyIdea.text: Animate main motion first, then offset secondary keys progressively and soften curves to create natural damping.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Animating Follow Through
Step-by-step
1. Block main body motion and key primary poses.
2. Select secondary joints or controllers and offset their keys progressively later in time.
3. Use Graph Editor to soften tangents and add decaying oscillation to simulate damping.
4. Playblast and adjust offsets until secondary motion reads as a smooth cascade.
Key Takeaway

Small, progressive time offsets plus softened tangents create believable follow-through.

Concrete example — ponytail chain
• Root follows body at frames 10, 20.
• Mid joint keys at frames 12, 22 (offset +2).
• Tip keys at frames 14, 24 (offset +4) with softer tangents and small oscillation keys after stop.
Use copy/paste offset in the Graph Editor to apply consistent delays and then tweak amplitude per segment for natural variation.

screens.title: Hands-on: Bouncing Ball Exercise
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll combine the principles in a single hands-on exercise that mirrors the chapter's recommended activity. Create a new Maya scene and add a Polygon Sphere. Block a 48-frame bouncing animation using Translate Y so the ball hits the ground and rebounds 2–3 times. For the first bounce add Anticipation: a slight upward movement and stretch a few frames before the ball drops so it reads as preparing to fall. At each impact frame add Squash by decreasing Scale Y to about 0.7 and increasing Scale X and Scale Z to about 1.2; place neutral scale keys before and after the impact to make the deformation a quick impulse. For Follow Through, add a small secondary element like a little tag or pendulum on the ball and offset its keys so it lags and then settles with damping. Playblast short loops and use the Graph Editor to sharpen impact tangents and soften stretch curves. The test: if someone watching without instruction immediately reads the ball's weight and feels the impact, your animation succeeds. Reflect: how did anticipation change perceived force in your first bounce?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Bouncing Ball Exercise
Step-by-step practice
1. Add a Polygon Sphere and block Translate Y for 48 frames with 2–3 bounces.
2. Before the first fall, add a small upward anticipation and slight stretch.
3. On each impact frame: ScaleY ≈ 0.7; ScaleX/Z ≈ 1.2; neutral keys before/after impact.
4. Add a small tag or pendulum and offset its keys to create follow-through and damping.
5. Use Graph Editor to sharpen impact tangents and smooth stretch curves; playblast often.
Quick reference
Impact values:
  ScaleY = 0.7
  ScaleX = 1.2
  ScaleZ = 1.2
Stretch values:
  ScaleY = 1.2
  ScaleX = 0.9
  ScaleZ = 0.9
Timing:
  Anticipation = 2-4 frames
  Offset secondary keys = +2 to +6 frames
Reflection prompt: How did anticipation alter the perceived force of the first bounce? Tweak and compare to see its effect.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn three core animation tools that turn motion into meaning. Squash & Stretch gives objects a sense of volume and elasticity. Anticipation prepares the audience for a big action so it reads as believable. Follow Through and Overlapping Action add secondary motion and realistic settling after the main movement. Together, these principles let you express weight, timing, and personality for characters and props in games and cinematic animation. We'll focus on practical Maya workflows — keyframing Scale and Translate attributes, using the Graph Editor to offset curves, and assessing timing through playblasts. You'll work with a simple bouncing ball and short examples like a jump or a punch so you can see cause and effect. A common mistake is changing scale on only one axis and breaking volume; you'll learn how to compensate other axes to preserve perceived volume. By the end of the lesson you'll be able to plan a short loopable animation that communicates an object's material and impact. Think about what emotion or weight you want a movement to convey before you keyframe; that intent guides every squash, wind-up, and follow-through.

By the end of these screens you will be able to name, implement, and combine Squash & Stretch, Anticipation, and Follow Through to make motion readable and expressive. The first objective is to understand these principles conceptually: know what each principle claims about motion and why it matters for weight and personality. Second, you will apply Squash & Stretch by keyframing Scale attributes in Maya while preserving perceived volume. Third, you will implement Anticipation to cue an audience with a small opposing motion that makes primary actions feel powerful. Fourth, you will use Follow Through and Overlapping Action to offset secondary elements using the Graph Editor so motion settles naturally. Each objective includes a short why-it-matters note and a verification milestone, for example a playblast of a bouncing ball that exhibits squash, a crouch-to-jump with anticipation, and a ponytail or flag demonstrating overlapping action. These skills are practical for game-ready loops and quick feedback animations, and they help you communicate intent clearly in short animation cycles.

This second objectives screen ties each skill to a short Maya exercise you can complete to verify understanding. For Squash & Stretch, the milestone is a bouncing ball with scale keys at impact and peak that preserve volume. For Anticipation, the milestone is a short crouch or wind-up preceding a jump or punch by a few frames, timed so the main action reads clearly. For Follow Through and Overlapping Action, the milestone is a secondary element like a ponytail, flag, or pendulum that is offset in time and settles after the primary motion. Finally, combine all three principles into a 48-frame playblast of a bouncing ball or a simple rig showing clear anticipation, squash on impact, and a subtle settle. Use the Graph Editor to refine tangency and curve shapes. These exercises are practical checks: if your motion reads on a quick playblast and communicates weight and intent without explanation, you have achieved the learning goals.

Animation principles are not decorative rules; they are tools for communicating physical and emotional information. When you apply Squash & Stretch, you answer questions about material and impact — is an object soft and bouncy or hard and heavy? Anticipation sets audience expectations so a major action is readable rather than jarring. Follow Through and Overlapping Action supply believable secondary motion so limbs, hair, or fabric behave with inertia and delay. Together these principles form a language: timing determines how quickly intent is communicated, deformation shows elasticity, and offset motion signals continuity. For example, a heavy object will have minimal stretch and a short, shallow anticipation, whereas a light object can stretch more and use a longer, more exaggerated anticipation. A common misconception is that more deformation always equals better animation — in truth, the amount of squash or stretch must match the perceived material and the scene's intent. As you plan an animation, state the intended weight and emotion first, then choose how much deformation, how long the anticipation lasts, and how much lag to apply in overlapping components. That planning keeps each keyframe purposeful and the performance readable.

Squash & Stretch is the most visual of these principles. It modifies an object's scale to show compression on impact or extension during fast motion. The essential constraint is volume preservation: if the object squashes vertically, the horizontal axes must expand proportionally so the silhouette's perceived volume stays consistent. In Maya, you animate Scale Y for vertical compression and Scale X/Z to compensate horizontally. For instance, when a rubber ball hits the ground, you would key a decreased Scale Y at the impact frame and increased Scale X and Scale Z at that same frame, then return to neutral scale at frames just before and after. When the ball leaves the ground, the reverse occurs: Scale Y increases for stretch, and Scale X/Z decrease. A common error is scaling just one axis, which makes the object appear to gain or lose volume and undermines the illusion of a cohesive material. A practical rule is to plan the maximum deformation, then distribute compensation across the other axes so perceived volume holds. This produces convincing impacts and elastic motion without breaking believability.

Let's walk a simple step-by-step process to add squash and stretch to a bouncing ball in Maya. Start with a Polygon Sphere and animate Translate Y to create a basic 48-frame bounce that impacts the ground and rebounds 2–3 times. Identify the impact frames where the sphere contacts the ground and the peak frames at the top of each bounce. At each impact frame, key Scale Y to a smaller value such as 0.7 and key Scale X and Scale Z to larger values such as 1.2. Immediately before and after the impact frame, key all scales back to 1.0 so the deformation reads as a quick compression. At the frames where the ball leaves the ground, do the reverse: increase Scale Y to 1.2 and reduce Scale X/Z to 0.9 for stretch. Use the Graph Editor to smooth tangents and give a crisp snap on impact with slightly steeper curves there. Playblast frequently to judge timing. If the ball feels like it changes mass, adjust compensation values across X and Z until volume reads stable. This practical loop will make the ball feel alive and responsive.

Animators often make a small set of repeatable mistakes when applying Squash & Stretch. The most damaging is scaling only one axis. That makes the object appear to gain or lose mass, breaking the viewer's suspension of disbelief. Another common error is an overly long squash or stretch — if the deformation lingers, the motion reads slow and gummy. Conversely, too brief an adjustment can be invisible. Fixes are straightforward: always compensate the other axes so perceived volume stays stable, and place neutral keys immediately before and after the extreme frame so deformation is a quick, readable impulse. Timing matters: use a sharper curve at impact to sell a snap, and longer, smoother tangents for stretches that imply speed and flexibility. For iterative testing, duplicate your layer or copy keys to compare 'without principles' and 'with principles' versions. This A/B comparison is powerful for seeing how much these small adjustments improve believability. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Anticipation is a preparatory movement that signals a forthcoming primary action. Think of a pitcher winding up, or a character crouching before leaping. Anticipation gives the viewer a moment to prepare and makes the subsequent movement read as purposeful and powerful. In practice, anticipation is a small, often opposite-direction movement placed a few frames before the main key action. Timing is the crucial variable—too long, and the action feels delayed; too short, and it doesn't register as a cue. For a jump, you might animate a brief downward translation combined with a slight compression of the body for two to four frames, then launch upward with a stronger key. For a punch, a subtle pull-back of the arm across one to three frames makes the thrust read with mass. A frequent misconception is that anticipation must be large to be effective. In reality, subtle opposition timed well is often more convincing than a long, exaggerated wind-up. Anticipation also helps combine with squash and stretch: a pre-launch compression can both cue the jump and set up a more pronounced stretch on takeoff.

To implement anticipation in Maya, start by identifying the main action and the frame where it begins. Insert a short opposing motion a few frames earlier. For example, if a jump's launch begins at frame 20, add a crouch that reaches its low point at frames 17–18, with slight scale compression and a downward Translate Y. Key all body or object attributes for that brief opposing pose. When the main action arrives, animate the strong forward motion and return scales to neutral at the peak. The key is timing: test 1–4 frames for small, snappy actions; extend to 6–10 frames for slower, dramatic setups. Use the Graph Editor to keep anticipation as a readable prep by shortening tangents on the prep pose so it snaps into the main motion. A practical workflow is to block the main poses first, add the anticipation, then refine interpolation. Remember that anticipation also interacts with Squash & Stretch: a pre-launch compression will make your stretch on takeoff more convincing. Misapplied anticipation that is too long or too large can distract from the action; always iterate with playblasts to read how the timing reads to a fresh eye.

Follow Through and Overlapping Action give animated motion natural continuity. Follow Through is the continuation of motion after the main action stops—hair, clothing, or loose parts keep moving and then settle. Overlapping Action is the principle that different parts start and stop at slightly different times; the tip of a ponytail will lag the root, a hand will follow the arm, and cloth panels will react with a delay. To animate these, you offset keyframes for secondary elements so motion propagates rather than occurring simultaneously. This creates the illusion of inertia and prevents staccato, robotic movement. For instance, when a character stops running, the torso stops before the hair and jacket do; the secondary elements drag and then settle. A common pitfall is keyframing everything identically so all joints move in sync—this flattens the performance. Use small timing offsets and softening tangents so follow-through reads as a natural cascade rather than a separate animation layer.
